paras: The threatened expulsion of the Soddy sect was a campaign of crowd violence and anonymous death threats in June 1888 against A. J. Brown, a Black man who claimed to be Christ, the white preacher G. W. Patterson, and their followers at Soddy, a mining village near Chattanooga, Tennessee. After a crowd broke up the meeting at which Brown appeared, posted letters ordered Brown, Patterson and several named families to leave within ten days or be killed, and the sheriff at Chattanooga sent armed men to keep the peace. No killing was reported, but papers across the country carried the story as a religious sensation that threatened lynching.

For several months Patterson, who said he was an ordained minister, held meetings at Soddy that drew white and Black followers. He announced that Christ would come a second time in the person of Brown, his helper, who withdrew to the mountains for a forty-day fast.

About ten days before June 20, a large crowd gathered to see Brown come out of the woods half naked, and Patterson declared him the real Christ. According to a Chattanooga dispatch, white and Black women embraced and kissed him, and "this state of affairs provoked antagonism." The later versions say onlookers rushed the sect: the New York Graphic credited deputy sheriffs with preventing a riot, while the Pittsburg Dispatch and a Chicago account described a fight in which Brown and Patterson barely escaped. The two men barricaded themselves in Patterson's house, and the crowd stayed into the night "stoning the house and uttering threats."

By June 13 ill-spelled warnings, one with a coffin drawn on it, gave the followers ten days to leave or "catch hell." As reprinted from the Graphic, the posted letters named "Old Man Thurman and family, Buck Thurman and family, Tom Black and family, Arthurs and family, together with Patterson and Brown." Other letters bore skulls, crossbones and coffins and ordered the leaders out on pain of death, with Thursday, June 21 fixed as the limit.

Patterson appealed to Sheriff Connor of Chattanooga, who went to Soddy, consulted "some of the colored heads" and ended the meetings. Excitement revived when Brown posted bills announcing that he would be crucified, and the sheriff later sent fifty armed men to Soddy.

The Graphic correspondent wrote that none of those named had left and that if they stayed "lynching will take place." No report of what happened when the deadline passed, or of any arrests, appears in the coverage.

The first reports were short Chattanooga dispatches that ran under headlines such as "Excitement over a Colored Crook" in the New-York Tribune and "A Negro Crank" in the Shenandoah Herald, which called Brown "the sable divine." The Maysville Evening Bulletin headlined the pair as impostors, and the Huntsville Gazette introduced its reprint from the Chattanooga Times as the doings of "two mischievous cranks."

Longer and more sensational stories followed at the end of June, carrying rumors of human sacrifices and naming a young girl who was said to have been offered, whose name each version spelled differently. The Indianapolis Journal's reprint of the Graphic, headlined "A Wild Story," mocked the "Ethiopian Savior" and wrote that the "orthodox mountaineers" would be as good as their word. The St. Paul Daily Globe ran the Pittsburg Dispatch version as "Worshiped as a God," calling the followers "dupes," and the Omaha Daily Bee summarized the Chicago account.

The versions differ on dates: the Chattanooga dispatches of June 13 and June 20 place Brown's appearance about June 10, while the later reprints call it "last Sunday" without a date. They also differ on whether violence occurred at the meeting, which the Graphic said deputies prevented and the other late accounts described as a fight.

reader.title: Threatened expulsion of the Soddy sect, 1888
bases: Anonymous posted and mailed letters ordered Brown, Patterson and named follower families to leave Soddy within ten days or by Thursday on pain of death, after a crowd attacked the sect at its meeting [A3][A5][A7].

No one is reported killed: a crowd attacked Brown and Patterson at the meeting and anonymous letters threatened death if the sect stayed, but the reports end with the deadline approaching and no killing [A5][A6][A7].

Separate Chattanooga dispatches and reprints from the Chattanooga Times, New York Graphic, Pittsburg Dispatch and a Chicago paper agree on the meeting, the threats to mob Brown and Patterson, the warning letters and the sheriff's guard [A1][A3][A4][A5][A7].

accounts.label: Chattanooga dispatches of June 13 and June 20
accounts.gist: Brown's appearance and the women's embraces provoked antagonism; ill-spelled anonymous warnings told the followers to leave or 'catch hell', and the sheriff was called to keep the populace from mobbing Brown and Patterson.

accounts.label: Chattanooga Times
accounts.gist: Sheriff Conner was appealed to because mob violence was feared, consulted Black leaders and ended the meetings; excitement revived when Brown posted bills announcing his crucifixion.

accounts.label: New York Graphic
accounts.gist: Deputies prevented the crowd from tearing Brown and his followers 'limb from limb'; letters named four families plus Patterson and Brown, and the writer predicted lynching if they stayed.

accounts.label: Pittsburg Dispatch and Chicago dispatch
accounts.gist: Outsiders interfered and a fight followed; Brown and Patterson narrowly escaped and barricaded themselves while the crowd stoned the house; letters ordered them out by Thursday on pain of death.

framing.detail: The New-York Tribune headlined 'Excitement over a Colored Crook' and reported the warnings while hoping 'serious trouble may be avoided'.
The Shenandoah Herald ran the dispatch as 'A Negro Crank', calling Brown 'the sable divine'.
The Maysville Evening Bulletin headlined Brown and Patterson as a pair of impostors and the Huntsville Gazette introduced them as 'two mischievous cranks'.

The Graphic story, reprinted as 'A Wild Story', mocked the 'Ethiopian Savior' and said the 'orthodox mountaineers' would be as good as their word, predicting lynching and 'the bloodiest massacre the South ever knew'.
The St. Paul Globe headlined 'Worshiped as a God' with 'A Sacreligious Tennessee Negro' and called the followers 'dupes'.

info: Brown emerged before a crowd about ten days before June 20 (about June 10); the warnings were out by June 13; the Pittsburg Dispatch version fixed Thursday, June 21 as the deadline; the New York Graphic version, reprinted June 28, said the ten days 'expires today'.
Soddy, a mining village a few miles from Chattanooga, Tenn.

A. J. (Andrew Jackson) Brown, described as Black, who claimed to be Christ; G. W. Patterson, described as a white preacher; and, in the posted letters, Old Man Thurman and family, Buck Thurman and family, Tom Black and family, and Arthurs and family; races of the families not stated.
No crime charged; the papers say the crowd was incensed by the women, white and Black, who embraced Brown, and by the 'sacrilegious' proceedings.
Described as 'outsiders', the 'populace', 'citizens' and 'publicans and sinners' in the congregation; the letter writers were anonymous.
No report of what happened at the deadline was found; the June 28 reprint said none of those named had left.
